articles.title: Five years later, the truth about Garland’s school board memo
articles.summary: A new Justice Department report reveals that the National School Boards Association coordinated with the Biden White House to prompt a federal investigation into parent protests five years ago.
articles.body:
Five years ago, parents across the country were angry and frustrated.

Schools had remained closed or offered only limited in-person instruction long after evidence of the damage to children was impossible to ignore. Mask mandates dragged on. Parents were discovering that schools had embraced radical ideas about race and gender that would have been unthinkable just a few years earlier.

So they did what Americans are supposed to do in a representative democracy. They showed up at public meetings, stood at the podium, asked questions, demanded answers and challenged policies they believed were harming children.

And for that, they were smeared, dismissed and increasingly portrayed as something more sinister: a threat.

On Sept. 29, 2021, the National School Boards Association sent a letter to President Joe Biden claiming that some activity surrounding school board meetings could be “equivalent to a form of domestic terrorism.” Just five days later, Attorney General Merrick Garland issued a memorandum directing federal law enforcement to respond to a “disturbing spike in harassment, intimidation, and threats of violence” against school officials.

The remarkably fast turnaround raised an obvious question: How much of this was already in motion before the the National School Boards Association letter had even arrived? We at Defending Education started digging. And through public records requests , we uncovered emails showing that the association had been in contact with the Biden White House before sending its letter.

What had been presented publicly as an independent plea from the nation’s school boards was, we discovered, the product of weeks of behind-the-scenes communication with the White House.

Now, five years later, a Justice Department report fills in much more of the story. Most revealing are the contemporaneous emails and records showing what officials inside the government were saying as this unfolded.

On Sept. 22, a full week before the National School Boards Association letter was sent, the White House Counsel’s Office forwarded the Justice Department an email from the association’s Chip Slaven to White House official Mary Wall that was, according to the report, “ in substance, the same as the final NSBA Letter .” The Justice Department was already discussing a possible federal response a week before the letter that ostensibly prompted it had been sent.

The records also show weeks of collaboration involving the association’s leadership and senior Biden administration officials. Even as the White House sought federal action, officials inside the Justice Department and the FBI raised serious concerns about whether federal law enforcement should be involved at all. They noted that the conduct described in the letter was overwhelmingly state and local in nature and that much of it was protected First Amendment activity.

One Justice Department attorney called the effort “ridiculous.” Another warned that if the Justice Department went forward, “ they might as well rename the damn thing the anti-MAGA Task Force .” Another observed that almost all the alleged threats were protected by the First Amendment and warned that the Justice Department was “ramping up an awful lot of federal manpower for what is currently non-federal conduct.”

The concerns extended to the FBI. One official wrote, “Not all who oppose school board actions or legislative decisions are Domestic Terrorists.” Another cautioned against treating someone as a domestic terrorism subject because of “policy or political disagreement with elected officials.”

The FBI ultimately opened 25 “Guardian assessments” — preliminary reviews of reported threats or activity. Six were handled by the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division and two involved its Weapons of Mass Destruction Directorate. The Justice Department says it is unaware of any prosecutions arising from those investigations.

Parents should never have to wonder whether criticizing a school board policy could attract the attention of federal law enforcement. Vigorous disagreement with government officials — even angry disagreement — is not extremism. It is part of citizenship.

There were, of course, legitimate threats against school officials. Threats of violence should be taken seriously and prosecuted when appropriate. But that was precisely the distinction the Justice Department and FBI officials were making: Criminal threats and acts of violence are one thing; protected political speech is another.

Justice Department leadership should have recognized that distinction from the start.

Defending Education is proud of the role we played in bringing the National School Board Association’s coordination with the White House to light. But this story was never really about us. It was about parents who were told that asking questions, demanding transparency and objecting to government policy made them dangerous.

Five years later, the public has a much fuller record of what happened.

And those parents deserve something they were denied at the time: acknowledgment that their concerns were legitimate, their rights mattered, and they had every right to speak up.

Erika Sanzi is senior director of communications for Defending Education .

articles.title: Cornell announces suspension of all frat parties amid Jane Doe lawsuit
articles.summary: Cornell University announced Tuesday it would be suspending all parties at fraternities through the end of the academic year and adding trained sexual assault investigators to its police staff amid the fallout of the gang rape lawsuit over an alleged incident at the Chi Phi frat in 2024. School President Michael Kotlikoff said in a…
articles.body:
Cornell University announced Tuesday it would be suspending all parties at fraternities through the end of the academic year and adding trained sexual assault investigators to its police staff amid the fallout of the gang rape lawsuit over an alleged incident at the Chi Phi frat in 2024.

School President Michael Kotlikoff said in a community-wide message that any fraternity that violates the party prohibition will be placed on immediate emergency suspension.

“There is an issue, post-Covid, of what are the options for students in a town like Ithaca,” Kotlikoff told The New York Times in an interview. “Many, many bars and venues went out of business and did not come back.”

The school says it will invest in “safe social alternatives” for students.

Cornell is also appointing a dedicated case manager to help individuals who report sexual misconduct navigate the process and adding more staff to its Office of Civil Rights.

Kotlikoff said the school also wants to change its social culture by accelerating recommendations from the Presidential Task Force on Sexual Assault and enhancing existing education for bystanders in such situations.

“Research has shown that campus sexual assault is not limited to the fraternity system. At its core is the specific context of social behavior and a deeply disturbing prevalence of alcohol and drug abuse. While this is not a problem unique to Cornell, we are committed to setting a higher standard for education, oversight, and enforcement of safe social behavior and citizenship,” his message reads.

The changes come after the school hired outside counsel to investigate its handling of Jane Doe’s allegations that she was coerced into drugs and alcohol at Chi Phi in October 2024 then raped by several members throughout the night.

The district attorney declined to pursue criminal charges at the time after Cornell police handed over a condensed statement of the situation that left out Doe’s statement she was “certain” she was raped.

New York Attorney General Letitia James is now also investigating the matter.

“We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe’s experiences, and those of other survivors. Cornell must be a place where safety is not an open question. I am committed to doing that work, and to seeing it through. It will take all of us working together, however, to build a Cornell culture of community, trust, and respect,” Kotlikoff concluded

articles.title: Cornell University bans fraternity parties for the rest of the year after sex abuse lawsuit
articles.summary: Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff suspended all fraternity parties after a Jane Doe lawsuit alleged gang rape at the Chi Phi house in 2024.
articles.body: Cornell University has banned fraternity parties for the rest of the 2026-2027 academic year in response to an explosive lawsuit from a female student alleging she had been sexually assaulted by seven men at the Chi Phi house in 2024. University President Michael Kotlikoff made the announcement in a message to the campus community Tuesday, in which he also pledged the school would provide "better support for survivors." "All parties and social events in Interfraternity Council (IFC) houses at Cornell will be suspended for the remainder of the 2026-2027 academic year," Kotlikoff wrote. "These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue." CORNELL PRESIDENT SAYS UNIVERSITY 'MUST DO BETTER' ON HANDLING OF SEXUAL ASSAULT ALLEGATIONS He added that there would be "zero tolerance for violations." Any fraternity holding a party or "social event" would face immediate suspension, he said. In the meantime, he said the school would be looking for ways to have "safe social alternatives." The student behind the lawsuit, identified only as Jane Doe in court filings, raised a series of alarming allegations last month, prompting New York Gov. Kathy Hochul to appoint the state attorney general's office as a special prosecutor to investigate the claims. Cornell also hired former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to conduct a review of her own. WHO IS SALLY YATES? CORNELL RAPE REVIEW PICK WAS FIRED BY TRUMP AFTER REFUSING TO DEFEND TRAVEL BAN Cornell disciplined some of the young men named in the lawsuit, but none had faced criminal charges. SEND US A TIP At least two of the accused men have asked the courts to have New York Attorney General Letitia James recused from the case over concerns that she tweeted support for the victim before her office was designated special prosecutor. ATTORNEY FOR FORMER CORNELL FRATERNITY MEMBER WANTS AG JAMES OFF CASE OVER POST SUPPORTING ACCUSER The alleged gang rape took place overnight from Oct. 19 to Oct. 20, 2024. Doe initially reported the incident to university police on Nov. 8, 2024. The school suspended the fraternity and opened an investigation, but Tompkins County prosecutors declined to file charges based on a six-page sworn statement signed by Doe that did not include the most explosive allegations in a reported transcript of her interview with detectives. When confronted with reports that she had made more explicit allegations about the case in her interview with police, Van Houten said that changed his view of the case.
